questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Equation Given a Complex Root and Its Leading Coefficient
questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-9+\sqrt{2}\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $1$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-9+\sqrt{2}\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=-9-\sqrt{2}\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(-9+\sqrt{2}\text{i}))(x-(-9-\sqrt{2}\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(-9+\sqrt{2}\text{i})-x(-9-\sqrt{2}\text{i})+(-9+\sqrt{2}\text{i})(-9-\sqrt{2}\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+9x-x\sqrt{2}\text{i}+9x+x\sqrt{2}\text{i}+81-2{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+18x+81+2 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+18x+83 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=2-\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $2$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=2-\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=2+\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(2-\text{i}))(x-(2+\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(2+\text{i})-x(2-\text{i})+(2-\text{i})(2+\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x-x\text{i}-2x+x\text{i}+4-{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=2\pm \text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $2.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-4x+5) & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-8x+10 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $4$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=-\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:  

$$
(x-\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i})(x+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i})=0
$$

   

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{(\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{5}{4} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}\text{ }\,\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $4.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $4.$ This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $2$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}))(x-(2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(2-\sqrt{3}\text{i})-x(2+\sqrt{3}\text{i})+(2+\sqrt{3}\text{i})(2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+\sqrt{3}x\text{i}-2x-\sqrt{3}x\text{i}+4-(\sqrt{3}\text{i})^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+7 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $2.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-4x+7) & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-8x+14 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-2\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=2\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-2\text{i})(x+2\text{i})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm 2\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $10.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $10.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10({x}^{2}+4) & =0 \\ 10{x}^{2}+40 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
